It is with heavy hearts that we share the passing of a true fixture of our department and community, Tyrone Wilkerson aka Ty.  For over 50 years, Tyrone served the City of Chattanooga Public Works Department with dedication, pride, and an unwavering commitment to making our city a better place for everyone. Half a century of public service is a rare and extraordinary achievement, and Tyrone’s hard work, wisdom, and warm presence left an indelible mark on his colleagues and the entire Chattanooga community.    This photo shows Tyrone celebrating his remarkable 50th anniversary milestone a couple of years ago surrounded by those who loved and supported him. He was more than a dedicated public servant—he was family to us all.   Our deepest thoughts, prayers, and condolences go out to Tyrone’s family, friends, and loved ones during this difficult time. He will be deeply missed, but his legacy of service to Chattanooga will never be forgotten. Rest in peace, Tyrone. Thank you for 50 plus incredible years.

Autumn wildflowers are in full bloom at East Lake Park! This hillside was previously turf grass lawn, which was costly to maintain and offered little erosion control or stormwater absorption above the park’s historic 90-year-old WPA drainage ditch. Inspired by the discovery of a rare Lady’s Tresses orchid on-site, the Natural Resources Team partnered with the Southeastern Grasslands Institute (SGI) to research historical flora and restore the slope with native meadow species. Right now, the hillside is blanketed with blooming Monarda punctata (spotted horsemint). Research from the Mt. Cuba Center shows that horsemint is an ecological powerhouse—not only supporting native pollinators, but also attracting beneficial predatory wasps that naturally control pest caterpillars and grubs. Take a walk to the top of East Lake Park to see the meadow in action before the seasonal blooms wrap up and let us know what pollinators you spot at the top of the hill! 🐝🌸 #chattanooga #cityinapark #nativeplants #spottedhorsemint #urbanecology

SCAM ALERT Law Enforcement scams remain a popular scheme for fraudsters. If you receive a call or text threatening fines or arrest unless you make an immediate payment, this is a scam! Hang up immediately, do not provide any information, and contact your local law enforcement. Law enforcement agencies will NEVER contact you demanding payments. In Chattanooga, payments can only be made directly to the city. Acceptable forms of payment include cash, credit cards, money orders, and checks from a local bank. Join the City of Chattanooga Team Chattanooga , a vibrant and growing community of over 190,000 residents within a metropolitan area of nearly 600,000 is known as the "Scenic City" for a reason. Our mission is to work together to build a safe, vibrant, and sustainable city for all Chattanoogans. To do that, it takes a team of skilled and passionate individuals. Co-respond with patrol officers to mental health and substance-induced crises city-wide. Balance immediate crisis response with ongoing engagement and support for people experiencing homelessness. Engage in evidence-based de-escalation and crisis intervention techniques while on the scene with individuals experiencing the crisis. Conduct crisis, safety, and clinical assessments to determine the appropriate level of care during client encounters. Proactively engage with individuals experiencing homelessness, building relationships, and assessing their needs. This includes regular visits to encampments, shelters, and other areas where homeless individuals congregate. Initiate voluntary and involuntary inpatient treatment referrals when appropriate. Engage in safety planning and provide outpatient referrals and resources to clients and their loved ones when appropriate. Provide short-term follow-up services including support, information, education, services, and resource linkage to clients and their loved ones. Provide education and information regarding mental health diagnoses, the mental health system, and accessing treatment to clients and their loved ones. Build and maintain effective working partnerships with law enforcement personnel. Attend all assigned departmental meetings, briefings, training, and collaborative meetings with local law enforcement, and community systems (mental health, judicial, healthcare, faith-based, educational) addressing mental health needs and systems change. Attend scheduled supervision with the Co-Responder Manager. Adhere to all documentation and charting requirements as dictated by the Crisis Co-Response Unit’s Operating Procedures. Demonstrate an ongoing commitment to inclusivity through effective working relationships with diverse clients, co-workers, and service providers. Establishes and maintains effective communication and working relationships with city employees, community partners/agencies, and the general public. Educates the public and law enforcement personnel on mental health and crisis intervention related topics through presentations, training courses, and other formal and informal learning opportunities. Completes crisis standards training as determined by the Tennessee Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse and other federal, state, and local regulating agencies when appropriate. Must be available for a 10-hour first or second shift and some weekends. Must be flexible as these demands may change. Must meet regular attendance requirements. Must be able to maintain good interpersonal relationships with staff, co-workers, managers and citizens. Must accomplish the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodations, in a timely manner. Performs other duties as assigned. This is a safety-sensitive position requiring a pre-employment background check, polygraph, drug screening, and fingerprinting. LICENSING AND CERTIFICATIONS: Currently holds a professional license (LMSW, LCSW, LPC, LMFT) or is on track to obtain one within six (6) months of employment. Mandatory Pre-Screening Agent designation is preferred. KNOWLEDGE AND SKILLS: Knowledge of and adherence to professional code of ethics; knowledge of Tenn. Code Ann. § 33-6-104; criminal justice system, its operations, and investigative processes; structure, function, mission, rules, and regulations of the Police Department, and the role of the assigned unit within the department; principles and techniques of inductive and deductive reasoning; mental health diagnoses (as identified in the DSM-V-TR) and experience working with individuals exhibiting these symptoms (e.g., substance use, hallucinations, delusions, personality disorders, post-traumatic symptoms, intellectual/developmental disabilities); federal, state, and local laws, regulations, policies, and procedures governing the involuntary assessment and treatment processes (e.g., 6401, 6404s or Certificate of Need); crisis assessment and assessment tools (e.g., CSSR-S); intervention/response (particularly in regards to the risk of harm to self or others); verbal de-escalation; and trauma-informed practices; community resources and their referral processes (including inpatient and outpatient services). Skill in computer and related software applications; interpreting, applying, and communicating applicable laws, ordinances, codes, rules, and regulations; speaking in public; applying independent judgment, personal discretion, and resourcefulness in interpreting and applying guidelines; identifying alternative solutions and establishing and maintaining effective working relationships with other employees and those contacted in the course of the work; oral and written communication; multitasking; computer operations. Ability to travel on occasion to both local and out-of-state conferences, trainings, and presentations. PHYSICAL DEMANDS: The candidate must be able to lift up to 10 pounds, wear a tight-fitting ballistic vest at all times while on duty, and remain in a patrol car for extended periods of time. Must be able to physically respond quickly to avoid danger, including the ability to crouch or kneel. Must be able to remain in a stationary position 50% of the time, traverse uneven terrain, climb stairs if needed, and be able to work in severe weather, including extreme heat or cold. WORK ENVIRONMENT: Jobs are sedentary if walking and standing are required only occasionally and all other sedentary criteria are met. Exerting up to 10 pounds of force occasionally and/or a negligible amount of force frequently or constantly to lift, carry, push, pull, or otherwise move objects, including the human body. Requires situational awareness in actively observing and anticipating potential hazards and risks and working with law enforcement to take necessary precautions that ensure safety. Sedentary work involves sitting most of the time. Jobs are sedentary if walking and standing are required only occasionally and all other sedentary criteria are met. This role will require riding in a police car for extended periods of time with a partnered police officer. The role will also require wearing a tight-fitting ballistic vest, implementing situational awareness, and the ability to work in various terrains, with potential hazards and risks, and in severe weather. This role is considered essential personnel, requiring potential response during inclement weather conditions. Chattanooga Police Officers Involved in Shooting, TBI Investigating CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) responded to a 9-1-1 call Friday that resulted in a man being shot. Shortly after 10:00 a.m., officers were dispatched to the 2900 block of Kings Point Road. Upon arrival, officers located a 31-year-old man with a firearm. Officers gave him verbal commands to drop the gun, but he refused. The man then fired a shot, resulting in a self-inflicted injury, and a CPD officer fired one shot. Hamilton County EMS transported the man to the hospital where he was listed in critical condition.  At the request of the Hamilton County District Attorney, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) is investigating the incident. The involved officers were placed on paid administrative leave per standard policy requirements. This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. #CPDnews

Person Killed in Wrong-Way Crash on Hwy 27 CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) responded to a two-vehicle crash that resulted in one death. At approximately 2:00 a.m., CPD officers were dispatched to a 0.5-mile stretch of Highway 27 northbound for a report of a multi-vehicle crash. The Chattanooga Police Department’s Traffic/DUI Unit responded to investigate. Preliminary findings indicate a Mazda CX-5 was traveling south on the northbound side of Highway 27 when it collided head-on with a Mercedes CLS 550. Hamilton County EMS transported both drivers to the hospital for serious injuries. The 46-year-old driver of the Mercedes died from injuries sustained in the crash. This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. Chattanooga Police ask anyone with information regarding this incident to call 423-698-2525. #CPDnews

In order to identify and keep track of individual birds, scientists put aluminum or colored bands on birds’ legs. Similar to the license plate on a car, each aluminum band is engraved with a unique set of numbers. This helps us track important data such as migratory paths, general health, and lifespan. CPD Seeks Community's Assistance in Lookout Valley Shooting Investigation CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is seeking the community's assistance in a Lookout Valley shooting investigation. At approximately 8:44 p.m. Thursday, CPD responded to reports of a shooting in the 300 block of Browns Ferry Road. Upon arrival, officers located a 16-year-old with a non-life threatening gun shot wound. Hamilton County EMS transported her to the hospital for further treatment. CPD's Homicide and Crime Scene Units responded to investigate and process the scene. The preliminary investigation indicates the teenager first encountered the suspect while entering I-24 WB from Highway 27. The victim exited the interstate onto Browns Ferry Road, and the suspect began shooting at her from I-24. The suspect vehicle is described as a mid-size white SUV with a Georgia license plate. CPD asks anyone traveling on I-24 between Rossville Boulevard and Browns Ferry Road between 8:20 p.m. and 8:45 p.m. and may have witnessed this to contact the Chattanooga Police Department at (423) 698-2525. Specifically, if you saw a white SUV interacting with a black Silverado truck. If you have dashcam footage of the incident, please upload it here: https://chattanoogapd.evidence.com/…/pub…/interstateshooting  This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. Join us this Saturday morning at Greenway Farm from 7 - 11 am for an educational workshop all about bird banding!  What is bird banding, you ask? In order to identify and keep track of individual birds, scientists put aluminum or colored bands on birds' legs. Similar to the license plate on a car, each aluminum band is engraved with a unique set of numbers. This helps us track important data such as migratory paths, general health, and lifespan. This is a FREE all-ages workshop. Please share with your bird-loving friends and family. We would love an incredible turn out for this fun event.

CPD Investigating Deadly Crash Involving Pedestrians on E Main St. CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. -- The Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is investigating a deadly crash involving pedestrians that resulted in one woman's death. At approximately 9:20 p.m. Saturday, CPD's Traffic Unit responded to reports of a crash involving pedestrians in the 300 block of E Main Street. The preliminary investigation indicates a group of people were using a crosswalk when a pickup truck hit two individuals.  Hamilton County EMS transported both patients to the hospital. One victim was treated for non-life threatening injuries. The other victim, an 88-year-old woman, later succumbed to her injuries.  The driver, Reginald Cousins Jr (DOB: 11/16/1966), was arrested and charged with Driving Under the Influence, Aggravated Assault, Reckless Endangerment, Vehicular Assault, Pedestrians' Right-of-Way in Crosswalks, Failure to Exercise Due Care, and Light Law Violation. Additional charges are pending.  This information is preliminary and subject to change as the investigation continues. Chattanooga Police ask anyone with information regarding this incident to call 423-698-2525. The charges and allegations referenced in this release are merely accusations of criminal conduct, not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted through due process of law. #CPDnews

Drives low-boy and other tractor-trailer rigs to transport heavy construction equipment and materials to and from work-sites; maneuvers equipment to load and unload from the trailer, operating mechanisms as necessary to position for safe transportation. Operates a jet-flushing/vacuum/viewer truck for the purpose of cleaning out storm drain and sanitary sewer pipe, manholes, catch basins and other brick and concrete drainage structures in order to maintain the flow throughout the stormwater drainage and sewer waste systems. Drives trucks with a side-mounted articulated vacuum boom along an assigned route for the purpose of picking up leaves, litter, and other yard waste from rights-of-way and out of drainage measurements in order to maintain stormwater drainage flow throughout the entire system. Inspects and prepares equipment for safe and proper operation prior to beginning work for the day; performs light maintenance on equipment which includes refueling and refilling lubricants; cleans vehicles, beds, and mounted equipment upon completion of assignments; secures vehicle after use. Performs basic and semi-skilled labor as appropriate to assist in the completion of maintenance, upkeep and construction projects; picks up paper, limbs and other debris; uses hand tools and operates motorized tools as necessary to complete the assigned task. May assist in contacting departments or personnel for an emergency situation. May be required to use, carry and answer cell phones, other devices, and/or two-way radio as determined by their job duties and their supervisor. Must meet regular attendance requirements. Must be able to maintain good interpersonal relationships with staff, co-workers, managers and citizens. Must accomplish the essential functions of the job, with or without reasonable accommodations, in a timely manner. May be assigned or reassigned to any division within the department. Performs other related duties as required. This position is deemed essential during inclement weather situations, and must report to or remain at work, even when administrative closings are announced, as determined by the Department Head. DEPARTMENT SPECIFIC DUTIES (if any): When working in Forestry division: Uses of chainsaws, rigging lines, pulleys, and cranes. Working in high traffic areas with the use of signs, cones, and flaggers and in the vicinity of power lines, moving traffic or directly above buildings. Removes and cleans up dead or hazardous trees. Available on call for storm work or downed trees. May train personnel. MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS: High School Diploma or GED and one (1) year of any combination of relevant education, experience, and/or training sufficient to successfully perform the essential functions of this job; or any combination of equivalent experience and education. LICENSING AND CERTIFICATIONS: Valid Class A, Class A restricted or Class B commercial driver license. Requires appropriate license endorsement(s) related to the area of assignment. KNOWLEDGE SKILLS: Knowledge of occupational hazards and safety precautions; general equipment and maintenance principles; materials and equipment utilized in assigned area of responsibility; demonstrated ability to drive and operate assigned equipment; operation of commercial vehicles that consist of self-contained specialized equipment. Typical equipment operated might include, but is not limited to: tractor-trailers, low boys, fuel trucks, bucket trucks, mechanical street sweepers, knuckle-boom trucks, articulated boom mowers, oil distributors, jet-flushing/vacuum trucks, CCTV equipped trucks and automated garbage trucks with an articulated arm. Must be able to use electronic devices to receive and track work. Position requires minimal, but daily public interaction and must be customer service centered, focused, and able to recognize or resolve customer needs according to departmental practices. PHYSICAL DEMANDS: Positions in this class typically require climbing, balancing, stooping, kneeling, crouching, crawling, reaching, standing, walking, pushing, pulling, lifting, fingering, grasping, feeling, talking, hearing, seeing and repetitive motions. WORK ENVIRONMENT: Medium Work: Exerting up-to 50 pounds of force occasionally, and/or up-to 20 pounds of force frequently, and/or up-to 10 pounds of force constantly to move objects. Congratulations to Lt. Jumaane Lanier, our Fire & Life Safety Educator, on receiving the Ralph Cothran Civil Service Firefighter of the Year Award during the 37th Annual Ruby Hurley Image Awards. The award recognizes extraordinary dedication to public safety and community service.  As the Public Education Officer in our Fire Prevention Bureau, Lt. Lanier holds a role that touches every corner of our city. If you want to see true passion in action, watch him talk to a room full of young students. Fire safety can easily be taught as a list of rules and warnings. But Lt. Lanier doesn't just teach rules; he connects. He speaks to children not just as a firefighter teaching them about safety, but as a mentor showing them what integrity, dedication, and leadership look like. It was a busy morning for the Chattanooga Fire Department as firefighters fought back-to-back house fires.  The first fire was reported at 8:47 AM on 10/13/26 at a duplex in the 1800 block of Citico Avenue in the East Chattanooga area. First arriving units found smoke and fire coming from the back of the structure. Firefighters initiated an interior attack and took another line to the rear of the residence where flames were through the collapsed roof. Searches were conducted and no one was found inside on either side of the duplex. Fire officials learned that both sides were vacant. By 9:10 AM, the fire was out.  Engine 4, Engine 5, Engine 10, Squad 1, Ladder 1, Battalion 1, Battalion 3, CFD Investigations, CFD Training Division, and CFD Supply responded, along with CPD, HCEMS, and EPB. There were no injuries.  As crews were wrapping up operations on Citico Avenue, another house fire was reported at 9:29 AM in the 1500 block of South Highland Park Avenue off Main Street. Callers to 911 indicated that flames were visible through the front doors and windows of the home. A plume of smoke could be seen by responding companies. On the scene, crews found fire in the front of the structure. Officials quickly learned that one person was home at the time of the fire, but they made it out safely. Primary attack was made through the front door and crews continued working to extinguish the blaze. Their efforts were made difficult by the amount of contents inside the residence. By 10:01 AM, the fire was out. One adult was displaced and will be receiving assistance from the American Red Cross. The cause of the fire is under investigation.  Engine 1, Squad 13, Engine 9, Engine 14, Squad 1, Engine 5, Squad 20, Engine 3, Battalion 1, Battalion 2, CFD Investigations, CFD Training Division, and CFD Supply responded, along with CPD, HCEMS, and EBP. There were no injuries.  Fire investigators do not believe the two fires are connected in any way. Thanks to Red Shift companies for their hard work and adaptability in moving from one response to another.

On Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we’re highlighting a powerful story found within one of Chattanooga’s most meaningful public artworks. At the bottom of The Passage at Ross’s Landing, a steel water spider rests beneath the shallow pool. Designed by Cherokee artist Demos Glass, the sculpture draws inspiration from ancient shell carvings discovered at the Dallas archaeological site right here in Hamilton County. In Cherokee storytelling, the Water Spider helped bring fire to the world when other animals could not. Using a small bowl she wove and carried on her back, she crossed the water, collected an ember, and returned with the gift of fire. Her story is one of courage, ingenuity, and perseverance. Created in 2005 by Team Gadugi, a group of Cherokee artists, The Passage honors Indigenous history, culture, and the Cherokee people whose forced removal is part of Chattanooga’s history. Today, we honor the Indigenous peoples who have called this region home for generations and the Native communities whose cultures, stories, and artistic traditions continue to thrive. The next time you visit The Passage, take a closer look. There are stories beneath the surface. #IndigenousPeoplesDay #PublicArtChattanooga #ThePassage #Chattanooga

HONORING OUR FALLEN: Senior Firefighter Chad Crisp was added to the Tennessee Fallen Firefighter Memorial in Bell Buckle, TN this past weekend. We lost Chad in 2020 after a brave battle with occupational cancer.  For the Crisp family, it was incredibly special to see Chad remembered in this way. His wife, Leah, wrote this: “While we honor Chad and his lifelong dedication to service, we also want to recognize the advocates who worked tirelessly to change policy so Chad could be included. Changes to presumptive illness laws at both the state and federal levels have started closing the gap in coverage for so many fire families facing a cancer diagnosis. Perhaps the most significant change is happening right here at home. The City of Chattanooga now includes comprehensive cancer coverage in its worker's compensation policy for firefighters—covering all types of cancer. To my knowledge, this level of coverage is limited to only a couple of municipalities statewide. Additionally, the Chattanooga Fire Department has implemented new safety procedures and early detection screenings to protect our firefighters. Chattanooga put words into action, providing meaningful support for firefighters and their families when it matters most. As we remember Chad, we also celebrate the dedication of those who continue to honor his memory by creating a safer path for those who follow in his footsteps.”

Childcare assistance can make a life-changing difference for families trying to work, go to school, and provide a better future for their children. The Tennessee Department of Human Services has begun inviting families on the Smart Steps child care waitlist to apply for assistance. We welcome this step. For families who qualify, help paying for child care could mean being able to stay in a job, continue their education and give their children a strong start. 📣 On the Smart Steps waitlist?  Watch your email for an official invitation from TDHS Child Care Services. Families who receive an invitation have 14 days to respond and submit an application. Approval depends on eligibility. After the response window closes for the first 100 or so people contacted, TDHS will reach out to the next group of families. These invitations are encouraging, and the need remains substantial. According to the Tennessee Commission on Children and Youth, 9,546 families, representing 13,835 children, were on the waitlist as of June 2, 2026. Behind those numbers are parents trying to afford the child care they need to work or attend school, and children who could benefit from quality early learning. Continued investment in Smart Steps can help more eligible families afford quality child care, keep parents working and strengthen Tennessee’s economy. Is your family on the waitlist?
